opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's natural for people to frame it as a race, but from the inside it didn't really feel like we were timing anything around GPT-4. Work on large language models at Google had been going on for years. PaLM itself came out in 2022, and before that there was a lot of foundational work: Transformers, T5, LaMDA, and so on. PaLM 2 was the next step in a fairly continuous research program. We were trying to get better multilingual ability, better reasoning, better coding, and a more compute-efficient model, not just a bigger one.

That said, I won't pretend the external environment didn't matter. ChatGPT, and then GPT-4, changed the public's expectations very quickly. Suddenly everyone was asking where Google was. That created a lot of urgency internally, especially around getting models into products like Bard, and later Workspace and other developer offerings. So the release cadence and how we talked about the work were definitely shaped by that moment.

But I'd say the main difference was less about the research than about the willingness to ship. Google has always been fairly cautious about putting these models in front of billions of users, because the reputational and safety stakes are very high when you're a search company. OpenAI could move faster and be a bit more experimental publicly. What GPT-4 and ChatGPT really did was show that users would tolerate some imperfection in exchange for a very capable assistant. That shifted the calculus for us too.

So, in hindsight, were we a bit later to market than we could have been? Probably, yes. But I don't think PaLM 2 was a reaction model built in a few months to answer GPT-4. It came out of a long line of work, and the bigger lesson was about how quickly you translate research into products people can actually use.

r001.rationale: The response says PaLM 2 was not timed around GPT-4 and that GPT-4 changed expectations, but it does not say OpenAI timed GPT-4’s release to precede Google I/O or anticipate Google’s planned release.

r002.rationale: The response says Google may have been later to market than it could have been, but does not state that an earlier release would have let Google claim the world’s best model.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think people read too much into the timing as if it were a head-to-head race with a stopwatch. From the inside, the cadence was driven by when the model was actually ready and when we had a venue to ship it into real products, and Google I/O was that venue. GPT-4 had come out a couple months earlier, so of course everyone framed PaLM 2 as the response. But the research behind it, the compute-optimal scaling work, the multilingual data mix, the smaller model sizes like Gecko that could run on a phone, that had been in motion well before GPT-4 landed.

What I'd say the timing did change was the pressure to ship rather than publish. A few years earlier, the instinct at Google was to write the paper, present the benchmarks, and let products catch up later. By spring of 2023 that was no longer tenable. The question had become, where is this live, and what can I use today? So PaLM 2 went into Bard, into Workspace, into Med-PaLM and Sec-PaLM, on day one. That's the real shift. Not that we were late or early relative to OpenAI, but that the field had moved to a place where a model announcement without deployment didn't count.

And I'd add one more thing. The gap in timing mattered less than the gap in approach. GPT-4 was one very large model. PaLM 2 was deliberately a family across sizes, because we were thinking about serving billions of users at a cost that made sense. Those are different bets, and I think history will judge them on more than who went first by a few weeks.

r001.rationale: The candidate says GPT-4 came out a couple months before PaLM 2 and rejects reading the timing as a head-to-head race. It does not say OpenAI timed GPT-4 in anticipation of Google I/O or a planned Google release.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not say an earlier PaLM 2 release could have let Google claim the world’s best model; it only says the models would be judged on more than who went first.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the timing of the public releases from the timing of the research. One model coming out after another doesn’t necessarily mean it was developed in response to it. These are long-running efforts, and the release date alone doesn’t tell you when the key work happened.

So I wouldn’t read too much into the order of the announcements. The more useful comparison is what the models can do, how reliably they do it, and how useful they are in practice.

r001.rationale: The response says release order alone does not reveal when the work happened and advises against reading much into announcement timing; it does not portray GPT-4’s release as strategically timed ahead of Google I/O.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that an earlier PaLM 2 release could have let Google claim it had the world’s best model.
